items.value: An AQI is of little practical use to residents of India's large cities, because levels there stay in the danger band for most of the year rather than spiking occasionally
items.reasoning: The passage states that an AQI is most useful where pollution is normally low but occasionally spikes, so that a warning prompts short-term preventive action. It then says this is not urban India: levels in many large Indian cities stay above every standard for a large part of the year, and an index stuck on 'Red' day after day leaves nothing anyone can do but ignore it. That is exactly option C. Option A blames governments and option D prescribes public awareness, neither of which the passage discusses; option B ('absolutely no need for air quality indices in our country') overshoots, since the passage criticises the index's usefulness in the worst cities, not the instrument itself.

items.value: India must create conditions for faster growth of productive non-farm jobs while simultaneously raising agricultural productivity
items.reasoning: The passage makes two moves: the number of people dependent on agriculture must shrink if per capita farm incomes are to rise substantially, and the non-farm alternatives are currently inadequate (industry is generating low-productivity unorganized-sector jobs, and high-productivity service employment is growing slowly). Option C carries both halves — productive jobs outside agriculture, plus improved agricultural productivity. Option A takes only the services half and ignores agriculture. Option B is contradicted by the text, which says manufacturing jobs are largely low-productivity, so it cannot be described as shifting workers to a 'highly productive manufacturing' sector. Option D discusses hybrid and GM crops, which the passage never mentions.

items.value: Biodiversity-enhancing (ecoagricultural) practices can often raise farm output and income while reducing vulnerability to disasters
items.reasoning: Every example in the passage supports the hedged claim in option A: ecoagricultural farms suffered 58-99 per cent less hurricane damage than conventional ones (reduced vulnerability to disaster), windbreaks and fencerows raised pasture and coffee income, proximity to natural habitat improves bee pollination for the 87 per cent of leading crops that need animal pollinators, and silvopastoral systems increase and diversify farmers' income. Option B reverses the passage's direction. Option C concerns permitting ecoagriculture inside protected areas, whereas the passage is about encouraging biodiversity outside them. Option D's unqualified 'yield will be very high' is far stronger than anything the evidence supports.

items.value: India should raise public investment and encourage private investment in R&D, technology upgradation and skills, since the sectors it must capture are high-technology and capital-intensive
items.reasoning: The passage says Indian manufacturing must move to higher-tech, higher value-added and higher-productivity sectors, that high-tech industries are mainly capital and technology intensive, and that the global sectors with rising demand are largely of that kind. The action that follows is building exactly those capabilities — technology and capital — which is option C. Option A misreads the text: the passage's whole premise is that Indian manufacturing is still at the lower value-added, lower productivity end, not that it already displays high value-added. Option B's 'not possible' is a defeatism the passage never expresses; it sets promotion of such manufacturing as the goal. Option D is contradicted outright, since the passage says India *needs to* capture those global markets, i.e. it has not already done so.

items.value: Because record production and full granaries coexist with mass undernutrition, the farm-to-fork value chain must be made more efficient to cut poverty and malnutrition
items.reasoning: The passage sets a deliberate contrast: India is among the world's top producers of rice, wheat, milk, fruits and vegetables and holds huge procured stocks, yet still houses a quarter of the world's undernourished people, and food eats up almost half the spending of nearly half of households. Output is therefore not the binding constraint — what happens between the farm and the plate is, which is option A. Option B's 'automatically eliminate' is refuted by the passage itself, since production has already risen without eliminating undernutrition. Option C misstates the passage, which reports record production, not that productivity is high enough to stop improving. Option D introduces welfare funding, which the passage never raises, and again claims outright elimination.

items.value: A strong Centre is the binding force that holds the units together and preserves national integrity
items.reasoning: In the metaphor the Centre is the thread, and the single consequence drawn is that if the thread snaps the pearls scatter — that is, without a holding Centre the units fall apart. This is precisely the view that a strong Centre binds the nation together, option B. Option A adds 'strong States', a claim the metaphor does not make: pearls are held, they do not hold. Option C reverses the sentiment, treating the Centre as an obstacle rather than the necessary binder. Option D makes State autonomy the prerequisite, which the metaphor subordinates to the Centre's unifying role.

items.value: Legitimate government rests on the consent of the governed, including the poorest
items.reasoning: The statement's argument is that every man who is to live under a government ought first, by his own consent, to put himself under it, and that a man who has had no voice in doing so is not strictly bound by that government. That is a direct argument for rule by the consent of the governed, option B. The reference to 'the poorest he' establishes who is entitled to that consent; it is not a claim about redistributing wealth (option A), about the poor ruling (option C), or about dispossessing the rich (option D), none of which the passage proposes.

items.value: 0.80 inch on the fifth day (six-day total 3.00 minus first-four total 1.60 leaves 1.40 shared 4:3, giving 0.80 and 0.60)
items.reasoning: The first four days average 0.40 inch, so they total 4 x 0.40 = 1.60 inch. All six days average 0.50 inch, so they total 6 x 0.50 = 3.00 inch. The last two days therefore account for 3.00 - 1.60 = 1.40 inch. Splitting 1.40 in the ratio 4 : 3 gives one part = 1.40 / 7 = 0.20, so the fifth day had 4 x 0.20 = 0.80 inch and the sixth 3 x 0.20 = 0.60 inch. Note the booklet prints decimals with a raised middle dot, so 0.40 and 0.50 are four-tenths and one-half.

items.value: Lecturer B is specialized in Geography (and is therefore the Kanpur lecturer)
items.reasoning: Fix what is given: C is Delhi/Sociology, F is Srinagar/Commerce, G is Chennai/Statistics, D is from Shillong, A teaches Economics. That leaves Hyderabad, Kanpur and Mumbai for A, B and E. A cannot be from Hyderabad (clue 5) and cannot be from Kanpur, because the Kanpur lecturer teaches Geography while A teaches Economics, so A is from Mumbai. The remaining subjects for B, D and E are History, Geography and Mathematics; since B teaches neither History nor Mathematics, B must teach Geography. B is therefore the Kanpur lecturer. A brute-force check of all assignments confirms exactly two consistent solutions, differing only in whether D or E takes History versus Mathematics, and B is the Geography lecturer in both.

items.value: The Economics lecturer is A, who belongs to Mumbai
items.reasoning: A is the Economics lecturer by clue 5. The cities Delhi, Shillong, Srinagar and Chennai are already taken by C, D, F and G, leaving Hyderabad, Kanpur and Mumbai for A, B and E. Clue 5 rules out Hyderabad for A, and Kanpur is ruled out because the Kanpur lecturer teaches Geography, not Economics. Mumbai is the only city left for A, so option B is correct and the 'cannot be determined' option is not needed.

items.value: Lecturer E belongs to Hyderabad
items.reasoning: After the fixed assignments (C-Delhi, D-Shillong, F-Srinagar, G-Chennai), only Hyderabad, Kanpur and Mumbai remain, for A, B and E. B teaches neither History nor Mathematics, and with Economics, Commerce, Sociology and Statistics already assigned elsewhere, B must teach Geography and so must be the Kanpur lecturer. That leaves Hyderabad for E. The city assignment is fully determined even though D's and E's subjects are not, so option D is wrong.

items.value: B teaches the most, with five subjects — Hindi, English, Geography, History and French
items.reasoning: Each statement assigns both named subjects to both named teachers. So B picks up Hindi and English from the first pair, English and Geography from the second, and History and French from the fourth, giving B five distinct subjects. A gets Hindi and English from the first pair plus Mathematics and Hindi from the third, i.e. three distinct subjects. C teaches English and Geography, D teaches Mathematics and Hindi, and E teaches History and French — two each. B's five is the maximum.

items.value: 45 — attained by 94 divided by 49, which gives quotient 1 and remainder 45
items.reasoning: Write the number as 10a + b and its reverse as 10b + a. When the quotient is 1 the remainder is the difference, 9(a - b), and the quotient stays 1 only while 10a + b is less than twice 10b + a, i.e. while 8a is less than 19b. The largest gap a - b satisfying that is a = 9, b = 4 (72 is less than 76), giving 94 - 49 = 45. A quotient of 2 or more gives a remainder of 8a - 19b, which peaks far lower (91 divided by 19 leaves 15, 83 divided by 38 leaves 7). An exhaustive check of all 2-digit numbers confirms 45 is the maximum, and the same maximum holds whether or not the reversed value is required to remain a 2-digit number.

items.value: Total monthly income is 42,000 rupees — X earns 24,000 and Y earns 18,000
items.reasoning: Let the incomes be 4k and 3k and the expenses 3m and 2m. Equal savings of 6,000 give 4k - 3m = 6000 and 3k - 2m = 6000. Multiplying the first by 2 and the second by 3 and subtracting yields k = 6000, and substituting back gives m = 6000. So the incomes are 24,000 and 18,000, the expenses 18,000 and 12,000, and each saves exactly 6,000 as required. The total monthly income is 24,000 + 18,000 = 42,000 rupees.

items.value: 4 metres from the ceiling (1 squared + 8 squared + 4 squared = 81 = 9 squared)
items.reasoning: The two walls and the ceiling meet at right angles at P, so treat P as the origin of three mutually perpendicular axes; the fly's distances from the two walls and from the ceiling are its three coordinates. With distances 1 m and 8 m from the two walls and an unknown distance z from the ceiling, the distance from P satisfies 1 squared + 8 squared + z squared = 9 squared. That gives 1 + 64 + z squared = 81, so z squared = 16 and z = 4 metres.

items.value: Station D lies on every C-to-H route (D is the only station with a passage into H) — but so does E, since C's only exit is A and A's only exit is E; both options are literally correct
items.reasoning: There are exactly two routes from C to H: C-A-E-D-H and C-A-E-G-B-F-D-H. Comparing them, the stations common to both are A, E and D. Of the four options only G and F can be eliminated, because each appears on the longer route alone. Both D and E are genuinely unavoidable: the only passage into H is the one-way D to H, and the only exit from C is C to A, whose only exit in turn is A to E. The item therefore prints two correct options and is defective as set. D is offered here as the discriminating answer, since it turns on reading the direction of the one-way list (the same fact the neighbouring question uses in reverse, H's only exit being H to G), whereas E is unavoidable from almost anywhere in this graph and would make the question near-content-free. E (option B) is the runner-up and wins if the setter keyed the forced first two steps out of C instead.

items.value: 4 routes — F-D-E-A, F-D-E-C-A, F-D-E-G-C-A and F-D-H-G-C-A
items.reasoning: F's only outgoing passage is to D (B to F is one-way into F), so every route starts F-D. From D the live onward moves are D-E and D-H. Via E, the choices are E-A (reaching A directly), E-C followed by C-A, and E-G followed by G-C-A, while E-G-B dead-ends because B leads only back to F and G. Via H, the forced continuation is H-G, then G-C-A, with G-B again dead-ending. That is 3 + 1 = 4 distinct routes with no station repeated, and an exhaustive enumeration confirms the count.

items.value: Station A need not be passed through; the sole H-to-C route with G-C closed is H-G-B-F-D-E-C
items.reasoning: H's only exit is the one-way H to G. With the G-to-C passage closed, G's only remaining onward move is G to B, from which the only progress is B to F, then F to D. From D the moves are D-H (already visited) and D-E, and from E the passage E to C completes the journey. So the unique route is H-G-B-F-D-E-C, which uses E, D and B (options A, B and D) and never uses A. A is in fact a dead end here, since A's only exit leads back to E.

items.value: None of the above — there are 13 such 2-digit numbers (12 if the reversal must also be 2-digit, 7 if the difference must be +27 in that order), and no reading yields 3, 4 or 5
items.reasoning: For a 2-digit number 10a + b the difference from its reversal is 9(a - b) in magnitude, so a difference of 27 requires the digits to differ by 3. Counting all such 2-digit numbers gives 13: 30, 41, 52, 63, 74, 85, 96 and 14, 25, 36, 47, 58, 69. Restricting to cases where the reversal is itself a 2-digit number (dropping 30) leaves 12, and requiring the number itself to be the larger, so that number minus reversal equals exactly +27, leaves 7. Every defensible reading exceeds 5, so none of the printed counts 3, 4 or 5 can be right and 'None of the above' is the answer.
